parts:
Hi Lance,

It will generally be the case that if you change the model for one of the parameters (lambda, phi, or p), it will affect the estimates of the others. For example, think about the different abundance estimates you might get in models with and without an important covariate of detection probability.

I can't explain the results you are seeing for your specific dataset, but the reason for the density estimator given in our Ecology paper is that we considered the case where lambda is the expected size of the super-population (the number of individuals that could have used the plot during the sampling period). You can't just divide lambda by area because the super-population is associated with an area larger than the plot area. However, under random temporary emigration, the number of individuals expected to occur on the plot during a short time period is E[N] = lambda*phi, so density is E[N]/area. Note that this estimator does not apply to situations where "availability" is related to processes other than temporary emigration. i.e. the interpretation of phi is specific to the study and species.

Richard

From: "L.B. McNew" <lbm...@gmail.com>
To: unma...@googlegroups.com
Date: 09/07/2012 07:15 PM
Subject: [unmarked] Open N-mixture model: Same covariate for phi and lambda
Sent by: unma...@googlegroups.com




Dear unmarked developers and users,

I have been applying the Open N-mixture models that allow for temporary emigration (Chandler et al. 2011). A model in which
a key habitat covariate affects both lambda and phi is most parsimonious and indicates that lambda increases with the
covariate while availability decreases. Imagine lambda for a grassland obligate increasing with proportion of the plot
in grasssland, while availability decreasing with grassland cover (due to larger activity areas in larger grasslands?).

Why do models in which both lambda and phi are fitted to the same covariate drastically alter the effect size of
that covariate on lambda?  In my situation, a model where availability is completely  random results almost no effect of
the covariate on lambda, whereas a model that allows phi to vary with the covariate results in a significantly
positive effect on lambda.  Biologically, I expect abundance to increase with the covariate, and the predictions for lambda
from the parsimonious model match my expectations. However, calculating density as lambda*phi/plot.area (Chandler et. al 2011)
results in unrealistically low density estimates and relatively no effect of the covariate on density itself because phi
decreases with the covariate while lambda increases.  This brings me to my final question.
Why is density calculated in an ad-hoc manner (phi*lambda/plot.area) when phi is integrated into the likelihood?
Shouldn't lambda already be adjusted by phi, as it is for detection?

My question can be applied to the flycatcher example analysis for Temporary Emigration N-mixture model provided by Dr. Chandler.
see below.

Thanks for taking the time to answer my question.  I appreciate your time and this excellent forum.

Lance



#Temporary emigration of Alder Flycatchers
